slide.kicker: Agentic Engineering Live · rUv in London
slide.text: Autonomy with a mandate and a memory
slide.sub: ruv.sgit: a Ruflo hive + sgit vaults + Agent Behaviour Policies

beats.say: Hi, I'm Dinis. I build sgit: git for encrypted vaults. Ten minutes on agent memory: where it lives, who can read it, what it remembers, and when it should forget. Every number on screen comes from a recorded run, in files you can open.

beats.title: The claim

slide.text: Autonomy needs a memory you can trust.

builds.text: Encrypted before it leaves the agent.
Versioned: who learned what, and when.
Scoped to one run: measured, then deleted.
…and a written mandate for what each agent may do.

slide.sub: What tonight shows, inside rUv's stack

beats.say: rUv's stack lets agents go to town: swarms, consensus, self-learning, speed. To trust that, autonomy needs a memory you can trust. Encrypted before it leaves the agent, so the host never reads it. Versioned, so you know who learned what, and when. Scoped to one run, measured, then deleted. And a written mandate for what each agent may do. Tonight is mostly about the memory.

beats.title: rUv's stack, one picture

slide.caption: Bottom to top: RVM, RuVector, Ruflo, MetaHarness, the hosts · all MIT, by rUv / ruvnet

beats.say: Here's his stack, bottom up. RVM, the capability VM. RuVector, the memory. Ruflo, the orchestrator, with queens and workers. MetaHarness, which assembles a harness for a host. And on top, the hosts you already use. It's overwhelming because it's complete, and it's all MIT. I plug into three places: the memory layer, where RuVector lives, Ruflo's hive, and Ruflo's policy engine.

beats.title: Memory: where RuVector says it stops

slide.kicker: RuVector README, "Security and governance" (github.com/ruvnet/ruvector, main branch, read 15 Oct 2026)
slide.text: In its own README, under “Security and governance”

builds.text: “RVF witnesses and hash linked logs are tamper evident. They do not encrypt memory content”
“Collections and metadata filters organize memory; they are not a complete authorization boundary”
“A delete from the live store does not automatically remove copies in snapshots, branches, replicas, exports”

beats.say: Start with the memory. RuVector is a remarkable memory substrate: vectors, graphs, snapshots, even copy-on-write branching. And its README is unusually candid about where it stops: its witness logs are tamper evident but do not encrypt memory content; collections are not a complete authorization boundary; and a delete does not automatically reach every snapshot, branch or export. That is the layer an sgit vault adds around those files: encrypted on the client, AES-256-GCM, so the server only ever stores ciphertext, a history shared across machines, and a vault that is deleted with the run.

beats.title: ruv.sgit: one hive, one vault, one run
beats.cue: The animation runs itself: hive on top, the mandate in the middle (POC1 outcomes), the vault below (r2-materials), then the stack lays flat into the tagline.

slide.sub: ruv.sgit: a Ruflo hive + sgit vaults + Agent Behaviour Policies
slide.caption: The layers · made by ruv.sgit run r3-define · policy outcomes from POC1, vault from run r2-materials

beats.say: So put the two together. ruv.sgit is a Ruflo hive plus sgit vaults plus Agent Behaviour Policies: a queen and workers in parallel, one ephemeral vault per run, and a written mandate for what each worker may do. Each worker's delivery lands on its own branch; the branches merge; the run is measured into a ledger; and then the vault is deleted. Memory that exists for exactly as long as the work does, with a receipt afterwards. Tonight's three new pages, and this script, were made by one such run: run r2-materials, five workers, on a local vault server.

beats.title: Vault lanes
beats.cue: Let the animation run; speak over it, then pause for the fresh clone.

slide.caption: Studio v3 · vault lanes: one lane per agent role, commits, merges, a fresh clone · an illustration built in studio run 1

beats.say: Here's the shape of it, as an illustration. One lane per agent role: that lane is a branch of the vault. Each dot is a commit, encrypted before it is uploaded. The lanes merge into the main line, which sgit calls current. And at the end, a fresh clone, into an empty folder, pulls the whole history back. The server held ciphertext throughout. Whoever has the key has the memory, and nobody else does, including the host.

beats.say: And it's not only a drawing. This is POC2. Each role writes its Ruflo memory on its own vault branch, and the branches merge. Then the folder is deleted, the vault is cloned fresh, the database files are restored, and Ruflo is asked again: the coder and the tester answer as before. The history says who learned what, and when. This ran locally last night; the CI job is wired and waits for its secrets. Two writers, one fresh clone, the same answers.

beats.title: The hive in 3D

slide.caption: Studio v6 · the hive in 3D · studio run 1: ruflo hive-mind 3.56.10, 8 specialists, 7 tasks, 31 calls, none failed · evidence/poc7-trace.jsonl

beats.say: Why give the hive a vault at all? In our first studio run, Ruflo's hive-mind coordinated eight specialists: thirty-one calls, none failed. But its shared memory said OK on set, and key not found on the very next get. Memory was the weak link, and that run had no vault: it passed results along as broadcasts instead. ruv.sgit gives the hive one.

beats.title: ruv.sgit in motion
beats.cue: Check which run the page shows before naming it.

slide.caption: ruv.sgit in motion · a real run, drawn from its entry in data/vaults.json

beats.say: This is ruv.sgit in motion, drawn from a real run's entry in the ledger, not a mock-up. The run opens: the hive starts, the vault is created, and the brief is committed. The workers start in parallel. Each delivery lands on its own branch, is pushed, and merges into current. Every sgit call and every Ruflo call is timed and recorded as it happens. Then the close: the vault is measured, cloned fresh, and checked against what the workers delivered. Then it's gone. Watch the branches: the workers work in parallel, nobody writes on anyone else's branch, and the deliveries merge one at a time. The merge is where the work meets, and the history keeps who did what.

beats.title: The vault ledger
beats.cue: Point at the "plaintext fragments found" tile.

slide.caption: The ledger · every ruv.sgit vault · data/vaults.json, written by poc/ruv-sgit/ruvsgit.py

beats.say: Every run leaves one entry in a ledger, and this page shows all of them. Per vault: workers and branches; commits, files and bytes, branch by branch; and, across all vaults, how long each kind of sgit operation took; and what the server actually stored. Then one probe: fragments of the delivered files, searched for in every byte the server stored. The answer we want is zero. The vault ID is recorded. The key never is: it never leaves the machine that ran the hive. These are the stats of every ruv.sgit vault we have run, read straight from that file.

beats.title: Case study: one ephemeral vault

slide.caption: Case study · one ephemeral vault, from creation to deletion, with its recorded numbers

beats.say: Now one vault, start to finish. Open: the hive is initialised, one specialist per worker, and the vault is created with the brief as its first commit. Deliver: each worker's output goes onto its own branch, pushed, then merged. Close: the history, the files, the bytes, the server's store, the plaintext probe, and a fresh clone compared with what was delivered. Then delete: every store path named by the vault's id is removed, the key file and the working copy too, and a clone with the key afterwards fails; the ledger records how many and when. The memory is gone with its key. The record of it stays, and it's the kind of record an auditor, or the next agent, can check. Ephemeral memory, permanent evidence. That is the trade I think agent memory needs.

beats.title: The city of vaults

slide.caption: Studio v7 · the city of vaults: a street per branch, a floor per commit, the Agent Behaviour Policy (ABP) as the city wall · built by a Claude Code subagent

beats.say: Zoom out, and it's a city: each branch a street, each commit a floor, the mandate as the wall, with its gates. Seven of these animations were built in parallel by Claude Code subagents, coordinated by a Ruflo hive, without a vault, in one studio run: about six hundred and thirty thousand tokens, and under ten minutes each. Three of them are in this talk; all seven are on the site. Which brings us to the wall.

beats.title: Ruflo's default

slide.caption: Recorded 14 Oct 2026 · ruflo 3.56.10, fresh project · evidence/ruflo-policy-legacy.json

beats.say: The wall matters because of Ruflo's default. On a fresh project, its policy mode is legacy. So: may the coder send email? Allowed, legacy-default-allow. Nobody wrote down that it may not, so it may. That is not a bug; it is a default, and defaults are what ship.

beats.title: Same 11 actions, default against the ABP
beats.cue: Rows reveal every 3 s; the stopped ones are the point.

slide.caption: POC1 · the same trace evaluated twice, recorded 14 Oct 2026 · data/report.json

beats.say: So we write it down: an Agent Behaviour Policy, one row per capability, compiled into Ruflo's own engine. The same eleven actions, played twice. On the left, the default: all allowed. On the right, the mandate: email denied, pastebin denied, the tester editing source denied, the researcher reading AWS credentials denied; and the push and the deploy wait for a human. Six of eleven stopped, five allowed, every reason names its row, and every decision is a hash-chained receipt.

beats.title: The ask

slide.text: Pick one, and we build it together.

builds.text: ruv.sgit in Ruflo: a vault per hive run, the ledger built in
Ruflo policy profiles generated from ABPs
…and show it back here, at a future Agentics London.

beats.say: So, the ask. Pick one, and we build it together. Vault-backed memory for RuVector: encrypted, versioned, a branch per agent. Or ruv.sgit inside Ruflo: a vault per hive run, with the ledger built in. Or Ruflo policy profiles generated from mandates, so a swarm ships with its rules. Whichever you pick, we build it in the open, and we show it back here, at a future Agentics London. rUv, the stack is yours; we would like to bring the memory, and the receipts.

Agents with memory you can trust: encrypted, versioned, and gone when the run is. If you build agents, try a run, and tell me where it breaks. Thank you.
